---
title: "Majority comparisons and expected ranks"
subtitle: "1.15 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 10, and Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.F"
description: "Relation between majority-win counts, posterior-mean rankings and expected ranks."
---

The majority-win count $H_i = \#\{j : \Pr(\theta_i > \theta_j \mid Y) > 1/2\}$ counts the opponents that unit $i$
is more likely to exceed. Expected rank instead sums the probabilities of being exceeded:
$\prerank{i} = 1 + \sum_{j \neq i} \Pr(\theta_j > \theta_i \mid Y)$. For independent normal posteriors, the
majority-win count gives the posterior-mean ordering. Other posterior laws need not have this property. The examples
compare these summaries with KRW's cards at λ = 1, where correct and incorrect directions have equal reward and cost.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Law on orders.** A beats B and C, each only with probability .51; B's one win is nearly sure (.99). Majority wins
  put A first, the expected rank B (1.52 against A's 1.98).
- **League.** Majority wins give the posterior-mean order: 0 of the 435 pairs differ. The expected-rank order states 6
  pairs against the majority; U13 is 8th by it (9.59) and 6th by the other two.
- **League, prior SD .30.** Still 0 of the 435 pairs; the expected-rank order now states 12 pairs against the majority.
- **KRW, race.** Majority wins form a strict order. Against it the posterior-mean order states 35 of the 4,656 pairs
  and the expected-rank order 62; KRW's card at λ = 1 states none against it, so no full ranking expects fewer wrong
  claims: 1,248, against 1,249 for the posterior-mean order.
- **KRW, gender.** Macy's beats Jones Lang LaSalle (.5008), which beats Dollar General (.5022), which beats Macy's
  (.5014): a cycle, and the three win 45 pairs each. KRW's card at λ = 1 (96 grades) puts Macy's and Dollar General
  in one grade, within KRW's solver tolerances.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
KRW call the grades at λ = 1 Condorcet ranks (Section II.F). Their remark there that the count of wins is equivalent
to the posterior mean rank (the expected rank) does not hold in general: on the race gaps, majority wins and the
expected rank order 62 pairs differently. The data describe KRW's correspondence experiment, not any firm's current
conduct. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), *A Discrimination Report Card*, American Economic Review,
doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version),
noncommercial use only. Pair probabilities as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW's code
(KRW replication companion) under KRW's archived pair probabilities ([KRW's cards along λ](../cases/krw-lambda.qmd)).
Changes noted; no endorsement by the authors is implied.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
library(postrank); r <- pr_case_krw$alternatives$race; e <- r$e[, , 1]
w <- rowSums(e < t(e), na.rm = TRUE); pm <- postrank_posterior_means(r)[, 1]; er <- postrank_expected_rank(r)
c(mean = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(pm, pm, "<")), rank = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(er, er, ">")))   # 35 62
```
:::

Standalone: [embed/majority-wins.html](../../embed/majority-wins.html), for example
`?data=krw&criterion=gender&unit=95`.
